subject: barnstormerBiplane
pitch:
Category: Vehicle.
Subject: barnstormer biplane.
Style: whimsical.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a whimsical barnstormer biplane for the SDK, needing a root joint for the body and a separate joint for the propeller so it can spin, while other decorative parts can stay as plain objects without joints.

I'm sizing it like a chunky exaggerated Stearman/Jenny—roughly 8m wingspan and 6.5m length—then laying out the fuselage, radial engine cowling with a lathed cylinder and bump ring, propeller with blades and spinner, and the staggered upper/lower wings with their gap and offset positions.

Working out wing extrusion geometry...

Working out the outline points for the wing shape with rounded tips, then planning the lower wing as a shorter, smaller-chord version with its own colored styling.

For the color scheme, I want a bright red body with cream-colored wings featuring striped red/white tips, computed procedurally based on spanwise position with checker-pattern banding near the tips, plus thin dark rib lines spaced evenly along the wing.

I'm also thinking about adding whimsical decals — a playful number or star emblem and text like "BARNSTORM BESS" rendered via SVG textures on the fuselage sides.

For the interplane struts, I'm planning two pairs per side connecting the lower and upper wings at slightly slanted angles, modeled as thin cylindrical rods near x=±2.3.

I'm also adding thin diagonal cross-bracing wires, and cabane struts forming an inverted V from the fuselage top to the underside of the upper wing's center section, factoring in the stagger between upper and lower wing positions and the fuselage's vertical extent so the lower wing sits just above the fuselage belly.

Checking strut endpoint coordinates fall within each wing's chord and z-range at that x-position, confirming front and rear struts stay embedded. I'm deciding to skip extra flying wires for simplicity and moving on to the fuselage.

Now I'm lofting the fuselage from tail to nose through a series of stations, each defined by position, width, and height, going for a chunky, whimsical belly shape with a separate cowl section up front. I need to figure out whether the loft function supports elliptical cross-sections or defaults to something else, so I'll just try the default skinning approach for now.

For the paint scheme, I'm leaning toward a classic barnstormer look -- cherry red body with cream accents, paired with cream-yellow fabric wings, maybe with teal wingtips for a playful twist.

Writing paint shader logic...

I'm adding whimsical character to the cockpits with dark oval cutouts and leather-brown rim detailing, then placing a fun pilot figure inside—tan sphere head, brown leather cap, goggle discs, and a trailing scarf curve in red and yellow.

For the second seat, I'll add a floppy-eared dog passenger if the budget allows, keeping things modest. I'm working out cockpit positions by raycasting down onto the fuselage surface near the upper wing's chord to find accurate placement coordinates.

Thinking through the Stearman layout: passenger cockpit sits forward near the wing center around z=0.7, pilot sits aft near z=-0.7, with cabane struts positioned forward of the passenger seat. I'm planning small tilted windscreens for each cockpit using thin rotated boxes rather than extruded shapes, keeping the geometry simple.

For a whimsical touch, I'm making the front passenger a dog wearing goggles, positioned so its head clears the upper wing. For the engine cowl, I'm lathing a rounded nose profile around the fuselage axis, sizing it slightly larger than the fuselage nose radius to give it a big, playful rounded look.

For materials, I'm giving the cowl a gilt-brass finish with a ring of exposed dark iron cylinder heads mimicking a radial engine, arranged as bumps around the front periphery of a closed, domed cowl shape.

Working out the radial engine geometry now — placing nine finned cylinders around a central crankcase hub pointing outward and slightly forward, with a spinner cone cap, while sorting out which joint the ring items should attach to so they don't accidentally snap to the propeller joint instead of the body.

For the propeller itself, I'm defining the prop joint position and orientation, then building tapered blade outlines oriented so their thickness axis aligns correctly, mirroring the second blade's direction vectors so both extrude properly. I'm also planning to paint the blade tips yellow near the ends to mimic a classic wooden propeller look.

Now I'm sketching the tail assembly: a brass-colored spinner cone at the hub, then a vertical fin extruded from a side-view outline with a separate hinged rudder part at its trailing edge, and I'm working out the coordinate offsets so the fin sweeps back with a curved leading edge before adding the matching horizontal stabilizer and elevators.

Simplifying the fin and rudder outlines, checking the rudder floats correctly relative to the fuselage tail height. I'm planning to paint the rudder with horizontal stripes using a sine-based pattern, then move on to defining the horizontal stabilizer planform with a fixed section and hinged elevators.

Setting up the elevator hinge joint along the x-axis, and now working through the ailerons on the upper wing's trailing edge, figuring out how to avoid overlap with the main wing extrude by offsetting the aileron slightly as a raised plate.

Still defining wing outline points...

Checking aileron thickness tapers against wing thickness to make sure they match reasonably at the hinge line, then working out the hinge joint definition and orientation vectors for the aileron attachment. I'm deciding to add ailerons only on the upper wing for simplicity, and planning the lower wing as a plainer surface with shorter span, slightly thinner slab, and a different color tint, with the upper wing positioned at z0=1.0 and lower at z0=0.

For the wheels, I'm sketching out a whimsical fat-tire look using a torus for the tire body sized so its outer radius sets the axle height, plus a smaller cylinder hub colored red with a cream center disc, and figuring out the axle position so the tire bottom touches the ground. I'm also considering what joint role to use for the wheel spin axis since "hinge" doesn't quite fit the available role vocabulary.

Then I'm working out the landing gear struts connecting the fuselage belly to each wheel's axle, plus a thin rod spanning between the two wheels beneath, and adding a small tailwheel assembly at the back with its own strut and tiny torus tire sized so it just touches the floor — confirming the main wheel's lowest point lands exactly at y=0.

For whimsical touches, I'm thinking about wingtip ribbon streamers with striped color bands using a sweep geometry, maybe a pilot's scarf, and ultimately deciding to add a small rubber duck mascot perched on the nose cowl as a lighthearted detail, built from a sphere body, head, and beak.

Now I'm placing the duck on top of the cowl and figuring out fuselage decals—considering a roundel emblem with a number "7" in a circle, and working out the orientation logic so the text reads correctly when mirrored onto both sides of the fuselage.

Decision made to skip mirroring on that side and accept the risk. Now I'm working out cockpit placement along the fuselage, figuring heights via raycasting, and sketching the dark cutout geometry for the cockpit along with a rim detail using either a scaled torus or a lathe-generated ring profile to get the right cross-section shape.

I'll go with a circular lathe ring for the cockpit coaming since scaling isn't available in the lathe options, positioned on the mostly-flat fuselage top with a sunk dark disc for the hollow. Then I'm building the pilot's torso, head, cap, goggles and scarf out of simple primitives, checking clearances against the upper wing by adjusting head height, and noting the passenger dog sits further forward under the wing with its own head position. Finally I'm sketching a bezier sweep for the pilot's scarf trailing back from the neck with some flutter.

Still writing scarf geometry and color banding...

Now I'm working out the windscreen panes for both cockpits, sizing and tilting small translucent boxes above each coaming to simulate slanted glass.

I'm adding exhaust stacks as short curved pipes along the cowl sides, panel seams and rivets on the brass cowling, and wood-grain coloring for the struts. For the wire rigging I'm using thin low-poly rods with a small radius and reduced side count to keep the geometry cheap, then moving on to the wheel chocks.

Now I'm planning the crossing flying wires between front and rear struts and the inner bay wires linking the fuselage root to the strut tops, placing two per side for a proper biplane rigging look. I'm also considering small whimsical nav lanterns at the wingtips using a glow effect, imported from the glow kit, keeping their colors flat so the glow renders cleanly.

I'm sketching the builder setup now: creating the root body joint, then child joints for the propeller, wheels, tail wheel, rudder, elevator, and ailerons, deciding which parts need explicit joints versus plain attachment. I'm working out the wing outline geometry and typing for the outline point arrays so the extrude calls for the upper and lower wings have clean, well-typed data to work with.

I realize automatic smoothing would be a problem here -- cutting a quarter of the way along a 7.4m leading edge would chamfer an enormous 1.85m chunk off the wingtip, badly distorting the shape. So I'll skip smoothing on the long edges and instead manually place rounded tip points to get the curve I actually want.

Writing the planform generator function...

Writing arc helper and wing outline logic...

I'm working out the wing paint logic, defining checker patterns near the tips with teal and cream colors, plus faint rib stripes along the surface. I'll make this a reusable paint factory so both wings can share similar coloring with slight variations, then move on to writing the fuselage paint function using a wavy pattern based on position and normal.

For the fuselage, I'm layering cream, teal tail stripes, dark red belly, and red top sections based on z-position and normal direction, then planning the body's loft stations from tail to nose and the cowl lathe profile with a rounded front dome.

I'm now figuring out the spinner cone and prop hub at the cowl's front tip, plus reconsidering how the radial cylinder ring should sit relative to the cowl rather than poking through it awkwardly.

Dropping the ring approach and placing seven cylinder heads directly on the dome's front face, angled forward to mimic a rotary engine, positioned manually with a loop since the ring primitive's orientation logic is too unclear to trust here.

That gives roughly 14 parts total, skipping extra push rods. The spinner sits near z 2.1+ with the cylinder ring around radius .38, spinner radius .16, prop blades around z 2.25, cylinder heads near z 2.0-2.2, and the cowl dome up front near z 2.05.

Working through the dome radius at that height, I'm placing the hub plate at z 2.1, spinner cone base at z 2.27 extending to a tip at z 2.6, and setting the prop blades at z 2.3 with a thin .05 thickness so they clear the cylinders ending at z 2.22.

Now I'm turning to the duck figure sitting on the cowl top. I'm casting a ray down onto the cowl surface to find the attachment point, then building the duck from a body sphere offset slightly above the hit point, a head sphere, and a flattened orange cone for the beak -- positioning each part relative to the ray's hit location.

Switching to wheel construction: a torus tire wrapped around a red hub cylinder with a cream cap, and I'm thinking about adding a whimsical hubcap pattern using a circular disc with painted spoke colors or a star design for extra character.

Now I'm setting up the tail wheel joint and strut geometry, using a small torus for the tail wheel with its own axle alignment.

Moving on to the pilot, I'm placing a capsule for the torso fitted into the cockpit opening, then positioning a spherical head above it, checking that the head clears the upper wing's underside.

Adding helmet and goggles...

I'm positioning the strap around the head and adding a small nose sphere, then thinking about giving the character a whimsical curled handlebar mustache made from small capsule or cone shapes.

Now I'm placing cheap capsule shapes for spikes on either side, adding the scarf, and considering arms resting on the coaming with capsules for hands gripping a stick. Then I'm starting on the dog passenger, placing its head sphere near the seat.

Writing dog head details...

I'll give the dog goggles too, and shape the torso as a tan capsule sitting in the cockpit.

I'm placing the dog's ears and small black eye spheres, then adding goggles pushed up on the forehead for visual variety with lens discs.

Now I'm writing the rod/strut helper function for building bone connections, keeping the color palette limited to a modest set of flat colors.

Defining ribbon curves for the wing tips...

I'm placing the navigation lanterns just past each wing tip, with red marking the port side and green on the starboard side.

I'm also sketching a small exhaust pipe sweeping down from the cowling toward the lower wing, giving it a flared iron-toned end to add character near the lower wing's position.

Shaping the propeller blade outline...

Still defining blade coordinates...

I'll keep two blades for simplicity, then move to the tail assembly: positioning the rudder hinge and fin relative to the fuselage tail tip.

Working out the stabilizer geometry, with hinge, fixed forward edge, and elevator aft edge positioned along the tail, keeping consistent y-centering with the fuselage. Defining the stabilizer plan outline...

Writing planform function logic...

In the straight-edge case without a trailing radius, the edge runs directly between the two corner points, which checks out. For the notch case, after placing the three notch points it continues into the trailing corner and then the leading arc correctly. The left side mirrors this by reversing the arc point order.

Sharp corner markers don't actually matter here since there's no smoothing applied, so I can drop that concept and simplify the point type to a plain coordinate pair. For thickness, I'm setting different profiles per part: thinner trailing edges for elevators, thicker leading edges for the stabilizer, and a constant chunky thickness for the rudder and fin to give it a whimsical look. Now I'm defining the hinge joint positions and rotation axes for the rudder.

Now I'm working out the aileron joint placement and coordinates, figuring out the polygon outline with rounded trailing-edge arcs for the aileron shape.

Deciding on the aileron's coloring, I'll go with solid red with cream rib stripes based on position along its span.

Checking that the upper wing placement, strut connections, and brace geometry don't create z-fighting, and confirming the ground contact points are the wheels and tail skid.

Now I'm verifying overall proportions—height around 2.65m from skid to wing/rudder top, length about 6m, span 8m, all fitting together well. I'm adding a glow effect for a small lantern sphere.

I'm placing decals on the fuselage surface, checking that the attachment coordinates sit correctly on the hull's curved width at that z-position.

Now I'm sketching an emblem texture using SVG—a circular badge with concentric gold and red rings outlined in dark trim, with bold serif lettering centered inside.

Writing builder imports...

Now I'm defining the color palette for the design -- reds, cream, teal, and fabric tones for the panels and ribbing.

Setting up the metadata and planform geometry for the biplane shape...

Still shaping the fuselage loft...

Checking the cockpit placement by casting a ray down at x=0 to find where it intersects the body surface, then positioning the cockpit ring lathe at that hit point along the surface normal.

Still shaping the pilot...

Checking the windscreen placement, I notice the pilot's arms overlap slightly with the front edge, so I'm trimming the arm length to avoid the collision, then positioning the passenger windscreen symmetrically on the other side.

I realize the dog's snout now pokes through the windscreen top, so I'm shortening the snout and raising the head position to keep it clear, then double-checking the passenger cockpit ring and cabane strut clearances line up properly.

Now I'm working out the cabane strut geometry connecting the fuselage top to the upper wing, and noticing the rear struts risk clipping the passenger cockpit ring. I'll simplify by using just the front V-struts for the cabane configuration like the real Stearman, avoiding the rear strut collision entirely.

Front strut at 1.05 and rear at 0.4 both check out within range, and the lower wing join to the fuselage at y=1.0 looks fine despite passing through it. I'm giving the cowl a brass panelled material with subtle rivets and polish, lathed smooth toward the rear.

Still writing builder code...

I'm checking the cross product of x and y axes to confirm thickness runs vertically, so the planform's trailing edge aligns correctly in the plan.

I'll keep the bevel at 0.012 since the tapered thickness should still work with that value. Now I'm writing a wing paint function that applies a checkerboard pattern of teal and cream near the wingtip, ribs at regular intervals along the chord, and fabric fill elsewhere based on position along the span.

Moving on, I'm setting up a lathe-based cowl geometry positioned near the nose with its axis along z, then continuing to add the lantern and remaining fuselage details, including extruded dog ears positioned symmetrically off the head.

Still writing geometry details...

For the strap, orienting the torus hole vertically with dir [0,1,0] so it wraps horizontally around the head. Then for the helmet, I'm building a partial sphere cap for the top in leather color, positioned slightly above head center.

Now I'm adding the dog's bandana: a torus ring around the neck plus a small downward-pointing cone for the triangular front point, and setting color values for the steel struts and wires. Then I'm starting the wheel assembly function, looping over left and right sides to create mirrored wheel joints attached to the body.

Adding wheel and hub geometry...

This gives it a nice dished rim look, with the tire bulging visibly beyond the hub disc since the hub faces sit narrower than the tube sides. I'll place a circle decal slightly offset from center for detail.

Wait, I need to check if the tube actually swallows that decal at radius 0.3 — computing the sqrt relation shows the tube extends to x=±0.146 there, which exceeds my planned decal position, meaning the hub would get buried inside the tire mesh. I need to shrink the hub radius and adjust its protrusion so it clears the tube at that radius, settling on roughly radius .24 with a half-length of .16 and the decal placed near x=.162, verifying the tube only reaches ±.116 there so the hub pokes through cleanly.

Now I'm sketching the tail wheel with a smaller torus and matching hub, adding an axle rod connecting both wheel hubs, then laying out the landing gear struts geometrically so they tie into the wings and fuselage correctly, and considering adding a coil spring detail on the front strut plus small brass bolt spheres at the strut joints for extra visual detail.

For final assembly, I'm setting the pilot position variables and casting a ray down onto the fuselage surface to find the seat height, making sure the surface query works correctly on the loft before adding wings. I'm also setting up the cowl surface query, then writing the ribbon and scarf sweeps using a color function that alternates red and yellow along a catmull-rom path with a box cross-section, before doing a final placement check on the remaining sphere parts.

Now I'm positioning the spinner cone and prop hub so the blades and cylinder heads sit cleanly within the cone's base radius without clipping, then moving on to write the actual code.
